utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that there was a preliminary matter to be raised and I do understand that it will be you, Mr. Ivetic, who will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, that's correct. I rise in relation to a request Your Honours made of the Defence a few days ago when giving the oral decision on the associated exhibits of Witness Radojcic wherein you inquired about two issues arising in relation to some associate exhibits. The first is in relation to 1D2153 and the Prosecution's request to tender that document which had been withdrawn by the Defence. We have no objection to the Prosecution tendering that document and it receiving a Prosecution exhibit number. In relation to 1D2149 and 1D2172, Your Honours' observations were correct, that they are indeed the same document. And we would thus ask that 1D2149 and its accompanying translation be entered into evidence. And we put on the record now that any reference in the statement of Mr. Radojcic, which is Exhibit D535, that points to associated exhibit 1D2172 be understood to refer to 1D2149 and the Defence exhibit number that that associated exhibit has or will receive. And that's all. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Madam Registrar, has 1D2153 already received a P number? I don't think so. Could you please assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2153 receives number P6955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6955 is admitted into evidence. As far as the other exhibits are concerned, I think we -- you would prepare a list or have we dealt with them already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, 1D2149 would receive what D number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I think that we have a written decision in relation to all the other Radojcic associated exhibits. Or it was an oral -- yes. I read it. I now remember that I read all the long lists of numbers. That's right. And these were still open. It's now clear on my mind again. Having dealt with this, I would like to briefly deal with two matters before we resume. The first is the communication about the Dobrovoljacka Street incident. On the 1st of September of this year, the Chamber asked the Prosecution to inquire as to whether any audio recordings or written transcripts of communications preceding the Dobrovoljacka Street incident existed. I refer you to transcript pages 25004 to 25006. My transcript stopped running. I do understand that we have to restart the ... Mr. Mladic, your voice becomes audible. I see that the transcript is running again. Therefore, I'll resume where we stopped. The Chamber asked -- Mr. -- the Chamber asked the Prosecution to inquire as to whether any audio recordings or written transcripts of communications preceding the Dobrovoljacka Street incident existed, and I refer to transcript pages 25004 to 25006. The Chamber puts on the record that on the 29th of October, the Prosecution, through an informal communication, advised the Chamber that they had, although limited, information that there may be an audio recording held in the military court in Belgrade. This is hereby put on the record. Will further attempts be made to obtain a copy, if it is there, is my question to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no specific knowledge about whether or not such efforts are underway. If that's the Court's request, of course we can undertake that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come back to this very soon, whether and with what -- how zealous we want this matter to be pursued. Then we move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, I think you said 15 to 20 minutes and then I said 15 -- well, at least a limited number of minutes remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of the time. Only I'm not sure that I would be able to finish everything in that short period of time. I'll try my best, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we can even save time before the witness comes in. I would like to call P3961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before we continue, I'd like remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Lukic will now continue his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have already called up a document and it's on your screen. It's called: "Instructions on the Establishment, Composition, and Tasks of the Local Crisis Staffs in the Prijedor Municipality." You see the title, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us take a look at the second page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 lists these local Crisis Staffs that are to be set up in the Prijedor municipality. We see three in B/C/S. In the English version we see the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then let us move on to the next page, page 3 in English. [In English] In B/C/S, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in the document we see nine local Crisis Staffs in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor. Do you know or did you know at the time that there were these nine local Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D827, could we now please take a look at that. This is Official Gazette number 2 of the municipality of Prijedor. We need page 5 in B/C/S and page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S version and also in the English version. We'll be needing the next page in English now to see what kind of order this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that something is being prohibited to the Crisis Staff. [In English] Of Serbian TO. [Interpretation] At the time were you aware of the existence of the Crisis Staff of the Serb Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if this is the logistics staff that supplied the collection centre of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was within that.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in this neighbourhood in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the name of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any one of these nine local staffs or of this Crisis Staff of the Serb TO?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my local commune, Tukovi, that's the executive organ. I was a member. And as such, I was certainly transferred if a Crisis Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether there were Crisis Staffs at the time in different companies?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such attempts were made. However, we asked for this to be abolished and to have only one Crisis Staff at the level of the municipality, that it wasn't necessary to have other Crisis Staffs established. Quite simply, they act as a hindrance in the functioning of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor, were there many Crisis Staffs at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was one Crisis Staff, the main one. I mean, what does "many" mean? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw just now --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the local ones, yes. But those are local staffs. They are not Crisis Staffs. They are subordinated to the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, and it also says in the instructions why it was that they had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement in actual fact you did not testify about any one of these Crisis Staffs. You only testified about the Crisis Staff, the main one that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on this document -- actually, we'll have to go back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P6948.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll have to show that to you first. You remember this decision that you discussed with the Prosecutor yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please remember the date, the 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a letter of the Crisis Staff of the 23rd of June, 1992, where it says that this decision is being forwarded for implementation.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In response to the Prosecutor's question yesterday, on transcript page 28872, in line 6, when you were asked whether this had been implemented, you said that -- you said the following: "We did not blindly implement this order."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now have to go back to D827. We are coming back to the Official Gazette of Prijedor municipality, issue 2/92. In the B/C/S version we need page 43 and in English 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remember the date, 22nd June. Under number 116 in B/C/S, and that's the document we see in English, it says: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality at its session held on 23rd June 1992," that means on the next day, "from that decision of the Crisis Staff of ARK Krajina," that is to say, the day when that decision was forwarded for enforcement, "on this day the Crisis Staff of Prijedor says: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor does not accept and considers null and void all decisions by the Crisis Staff of ARK Krajina taken before 22nd June 1992." Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that the Crisis Staff of Prijedor refused to implement the decisions of the Crisis Staff of ARK adopted before 22nd June?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that decision was made at one session of the Crisis Staff, and one of the reasons that was stated was that there were no personnel from Prijedor on the ARK Crisis Staff of Krajina, and also the provision that required all non-Serbs to be dismissed from senior positions. We could not accept that and we had to adopt this type of conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 44 in B/C/S and page 101 in English. Let us look at number 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two days later, on 25 June 1992, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality adopts the conclusion that the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff shall not observe any enactments adopted by the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So this is for the future. Do you remember this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe Kovacevic and another gentleman went for talks and adopted this conclusion in order to drive home some sense to the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P6952.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the CSB. And my question had to do with the contribution of Simo Miskovic regarding the Assembly of the Republika Srpska held on 29 May 1992, relative to your claim that communication was difficult until the opening of the corridor. You said the corridor was opened on a holiday, 28th of May. Does the corridor have anything to do with travel and the axis to Banja Luka from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Kozarac was engulfed in combat, we mainly took a bypass to Banja Luka via Maricka and other villages, to Omarska and on to Banja Luka. It was not advisable to travel via this direct road because there was still groups roaming around that area. Now, whether the police went there or not, I can't remember. All I remember was that it was risky to travel and we took a roundabout way via these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question had to do with the Posavina corridor. Was it possible to reach Banja Luka even before the corridor through Posavina was opened?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible. But I just explained how.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about Hambarine and you said you received reports that heavy fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe one thing remained unclear, so I'm going to ask you: You received the report about the wounding of one soldier in the form of a report, or you read it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally didn't receive any reports. Maybe it was discussed at the Crisis Staff meeting. But I believe such news were published in "Kozarski Vjesnik" newspaper, that one soldier was wounded, and Radio Prijedor was broadcasting constantly that heavy fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a resident of Prijedor, did you have information that there was combat even after the check-point was removed from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that the groups that had withdrawn from Hambarine towards Kurevo needed to be brought to justice and that was the job of the army and the police. So they continued to search the terrain to solve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now briefly about Stari Grad. Yesterday it was put to you that Stari Grad was destroyed for the most part. Do you know what the axes of attack were on 30th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the bank of the river Sana, from Raskovac towards Stari Grup [as interpreted]. One group came out of the mosque in the centre of town, other groups were going from Puharska towards the centre of town, and one group was coming from Gomjenica and made its base in my grandfather's house, which was completely destroyed after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know along which routes these groups withdrew, retreated?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were able to retreat. There were many wounded, many killed. I believe 16 or 18 of our policemen were killed. Yes, it's coming back to me. I believe they managed to retreat towards Bosanski Novi and Krupa, I think, if my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they withdrew again via Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the road. Those who came from Raskovac pulled out that way, and those who came from Puharska retreated towards Cerek again via Stari Grad. There was a lot of destruction in Stari Grad, that's true, but even in Serbian neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I had to ask you about Stari Grad for the record. It's clear in your head, but we have to have it clearly on the record. Therefore, would you say that heavy fighting went on in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, thank you. This is all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, Your Honours, I don't know if it's a good moment. I have one associated exhibit only to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 1D111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the order concerning implementation of the decision of the presidency of the republic. Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D111 receives number D829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like just one. If I can check just very quickly. I'm looking for more information in relation to another, but I'll just focus on this one for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic. You were asked by Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- at page 10 of today's temporary transcript - let me just find the exact quote - whether you received a report about the wounding of one soldier or just read about it somewhere else. And you said: "I personally didn't receive any reports." This matter was also raised in the Karadzic case, I believe, at page 45762 of the transcript of those proceedings. And -- let me just make sure I've indicated to you that this is in connection with Hambarine. And you were asked the following. First you were directed to a Crisis Staff statement. The question was: "And this is a Crisis Staff statement from the following day, the 24th of May, and in the first paragraph, this is just under the line in the English, at its morning session the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff discussed the situation in the municipality, and it says: "'Following yesterday's operations by the army directed at disarming the Muslim paramilitary formations from the Hambarine local commune, the situation had calmed down during the night. The Crisis Staff assessed that the operation had been successful. The army suffered no loss during the combat activities. One member was wounded.'" And the questioner went on to note that you had said a moment ago that you didn't have that kind of information, and then after that reminded that in fact the Crisis Staff the very next day said that the army had suffered no casualties in the Hambarine operation. And your answer at that time was: "I really cannot remember. It's been over 20 years now. Whether there were any wounded or not, I cannot remember. Maybe I didn't attend the session, maybe." Notwithstanding that, Mr. Mandic, you will acknowledge, however, that the Crisis Staff received reports about what happened in Hambarine and you might have been at that session but you can no longer -- you could no longer recall at the time you testified in Karadzic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But I believe that I read that in the documentation, in "Kozarski Vjesnik," during proofing. There was one person wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Kozarski Vjesnik" was an organ of the Serbian authorities at that time and the Crisis Staff issued statements via "Kozarski Vjesnik" and the one I just referred to was one of those; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Where can we find that "Kozarski Vjesnik" was organ of Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. This happens to be a cross-examination question to which a witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's misstating the evidence. There is no trace of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's keep -- let's calm down. Mr. Tieger, by combining the "Kozarski Vjesnik" to be an organ of the Serbian authorities and to ask about one specific example, you have mixed up two things and that may lead to confusion whether you are still seeking confirmation on both elements. The first question, therefore, should be: Was "Kozarski Vjesnik" an organ of the Serbian authorities at the time? Witness, could you answer that question to start with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, "Kozarski Vjesnik" was a newspaper, a weekly, that came out in Prijedor municipality. It was financed then and it is financed now by the budget of Prijedor municipality. Nothing has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps you now put the second question, Mr. Tieger, the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the statement by the Crisis Staff that we just referred to regarding its information about what happened in Hambarine was issued via "Kozarski Vjesnik" and that's what you were referring to when you said you saw it in proofing?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could have just one moment, Mr. President. I'm tracking down a document that I have in a different form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could meanwhile, if you do not mind, Mr. Tieger, ask a question. Mr. Mandic, we just looked at a document in which it was stated that the Prijedor Crisis Staff considered decisions by the ARK Crisis Staff to be invalid. Was the decision of the 22nd of June by the ARK giving instructions as where Serbs -- where non-Serbs could not work any longer or where even Serbs could not work any longer, was that one of the decisions that you had declared invalid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that also applied to that decision. Because we just didn't want to tamper in any way with people who were loyal, who were doing their jobs, and that was one of the reasons to reject this decision of the ARK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the rejection was in general terms, not on a specific document, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tieger switch off his microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that was one of the reasons. We simply didn't want to blindly follow something that was not consistent with our situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were asked about this decision by Mr. Tieger, and I'll read the question again. Mr. Tieger asked you: "This is a document dated the 22nd of May, 1992," and perhaps we should have it on our screen at this moment. It's P6949. Meanwhile, I'll continue. So Mr. Tieger pointed you at a document: "... sent by the Prijedor Crisis Staff to all commercial and social enterprises in accordance," as the document states, "with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- only it's wrong number. It's 6948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm reading from yesterday's transcript. It -- we are talking about 65 ter 17422?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's -- then I'm wrong, I thought you called another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. This is the one I called, 6949. You were asked about this document yesterday and -- no, I have made a mistake here, I'm afraid. So therefore I'll withdraw that question. I have one question remaining. You said you -- you said, and we read in the document, that you reject all the decisions prior to the 22nd of June and you adopt all the decisions after the 22nd of June. My question is what happened with decisions that were adopted on the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't remember. I don't know what decisions those were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be important because the decision we are talking about was adopted on the 22nd of June. So you wouldn't know whether that one was rejected on the basis of the decision we looked at declaring invalid or not accept decisions taken before the 22nd of June. Could I also invite the parties to have a close look at whether the translation causes any problems there, because it's a bit odd to decide on what happens with decisions before the 22nd of June and after the 22nd of June which leaves entirely open what is the case with decisions that were adopted on the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that'll entirely open up a question or two regarding that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just asking the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are two decisions. One decision is in regard of decisions --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger suggested --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let Mr. Tieger [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger doesn't give evidence at this moment. He says that he wants to clarify with the witness certain matters. And since it confuses me at this moment, and then, of course, Mr. Lukic, if this something is new triggered by the Chamber, then we are in the situation that you can ask additional questions as well. Mr. Tieger, if you think you could clarify the matter by putting further questions to the witness and drawing our attention to this or other documents, then that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, Mr. Lukic drew your attention to a couple of documents apparently reflecting some tension or friction between the ARK Crisis Staff and the Prijedor Crisis Staff in June, and Prijedor's reaction to that. Irrespective of those exchanges or those positions taken as reflected in those documents on the -- in that part of June -- and let me just get the dates, just a second. All right. The 25th of June was the last date I saw. So that's consistent with your recollection, sir, that the -- that this tension between the ARK Crisis Staff and the Prijedor's Crisis Staff was in the latter part of June?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were tensions, but it had mainly to do with the fact that Prijedor was not represented on the ARK Crisis Staff. That's the reason why the people from the SDS did not accept these decisions. They wanted our personnel to be represented in order to accept their decisions, because Prijedor was practically a part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and we did not have our representatives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And irrespective of those tensions, sir, by the early part of July, those tensions were sufficiently resolved that Prijedor was again forwarding ARK Crisis Staff decisions for implementation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we can look at some documents to confirm it. I'm prepared to accept what you say, that these problems had been resolved by then. I don't know how long it took, ten or 20 days, I can't pin-point a date. I know these problems went for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 65 ter 7148, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we continue to do that, I would have one question. You were asked about this yesterday as well, and you said: "We did not implement this blindly." You didn't say: "We rejected those decisions." You said: "We did not implement it blindly," which suggests that you accepted the decision as validly taken but that you did not feel bound in every respect to implement it, and that's of course something quite different from rejecting as invalid a decision. Now, which of the two specifically on this decision by the ARK Crisis Staff was the case? Did you not implement it blindly but did you accept it to be validly adopted? Or do you say this is a decision we bluntly rejected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was an official letter rejecting that decision of ARK Krajina. As for the part that I already cited, I meant that we didn't implement all the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you said yesterday. Yesterday it was specifically about this 22nd of June decision, so that's now a new answer. And if there is any letter which specifically addresses this decision, then of course the Chamber would like to know because then it's a relevant material. But, Witness, we have not looked at that letter you are hinting at at this moment, did you -- did we? We have not seen that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. There was a dispatch from the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality to the Crisis Staff of ARK Krajina. It wasn't a letter. It was an official dispatch. Mr. Lukic showed that decision of the Crisis Staff a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was non -- not specific on the decision we are discussing now, that's one; and second, it rejects any decisions adopted before the 22nd of June, it doesn't say anything about decisions adopted on the 22nd of June. But that was the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I cannot remember now the decision of the 22nd. I simply cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President. I had asked for 65 ter 7148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the clock, can we finish within a couple of minutes do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mandic, on the screen in front of you is a document dated the 6th of July, 1992, in early July as I'd mentioned to you, signed by Dr. Stakic, the president of the Crisis Staff, providing that the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka number 03-35/92 dated 22 June 1992 has been delivered to the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality. The decision is being forwarded to you for the purpose of its implementation. First question: That's a reflection of the fact that by early July whatever tensions you referred to earlier between the ARK Crisis Staff and the Prijedor Crisis Staff had been sufficiently resolved, that the Prijedor Crisis Staff was again implementing the ARK Crisis Staff decisions; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the way it is, most probably it is. I cannot remember right now how long it went on. And obviously the document says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Second question: Just in case there was any confusion about that June 22nd order that we've been discussing, this decision ensures that the -- a decision of June 22nd, 03-351/92, which we saw earlier and is now in evidence as P6948, would be implemented. And that's the decision about the personnel of Serbian ethnicity. That's correct too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot link this up, what Serb ethnicity? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just keep an eye on that number, 03-351/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And very quickly call up P6948.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the decision, which has been discussed at considerable length by now, of the 22nd of June providing that only personnel of Serbian ethnicity may hold executive posts, et cetera. And that, as we can see, 03-531/92. So the document we just looked at is an explicit reference to this decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd tender 7148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 7148 receives number P6956, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Has this triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Lukic? Then, Mr. Mandic -- Mr. Mandic, since the Judges also have no further questions for you, this concludes your evidence. We would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the many questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. We wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed. Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that Ms. Hasan wants to raise a matter before we continue with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. I just refer back to a matter that was raised by Mr. McCloskey the day before yesterday in relation to intercept P1366. It was a question about replacing the translation that was part of that -- the English translation of that intercept and uploading a new translation. While there appears to have been an agreement at that time, it seems that in the interim, when Mr. McCloskey spoke with the Defence on the issue, that my understanding is there is no longer agreement on that. And perhaps I don't want to -- I wasn't present during the communication between Mr. McCloskey and the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber would prefer to have an agreement between the parties on the translation, but if it's not possible, then what we need is then a formal translation or the translation to be verified on the specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The revised CLSS translation has been uploaded and it bears document ID 03205457-1ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's -- I then do not fully understand. Does it mean that the Defence does not accept that new translation? Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour. Just a few sentences. I talked to Mr. McCloskey about this question, and I was prepared to accept at any point in time that in the B/C/S text there is the word "five." We were asked to stipulate as to the meaning of "five," "pet," and that it should be marked with the letter A or the letter F. Unfortunately, we didn't manage to agree on that and we agreed that the text of the intercept should go as the original B/C/S says and that is "five." The position of the Defence is that anything beyond that would not be a translation but rather an interpretation of what the word "five" might mean, and that is how we left this pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have two issues: The one it's a matter whether it's an A or whether it's a 5; and the second issue, what it would mean if it were a 5. Is there any dispute about what it would mean if it were an A? Or is that unclear as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the original B/C/S text there is the word "five," "pet." What it would mean is still in dispute, that's the dispute between us and Mr. McCloskey. Because in B/C/S when somebody says "5," "grade 5," it can mean the best and it can mean the worst. So that would be prone to interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's up for the Chamber then to -- after having heard the parties to interpret what it means. I do understand that now at least there is no dispute about what should be uploaded, irrespective of how that should be interpreted. Madam Registrar, the number just mentioned by Ms. Hasan may be -- may replace the present translation as it is now in e-court for P1366, and you're instructed to do so. That's it. Then we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take an early break. We will resume at 5 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into closed session, very briefly, in order to have the witness enter the courtroom. Meanwhile, perhaps, Mr. Lukic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness GRM130, because that's how we will call you, you'll now first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With the assistance of the court usher, I'd like to show the witness the document that is 1D5302, but due to technical reasons it's not yet in e-court. That's the pseudonym sheet. So, Your Honours, I would propose that we reserve a number for this once the procedure is fulfilled - I have provided copies for Your Honours and anyone else who needs it - and then revisit the issue once the original is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to take a look at this sheet and please verify for us if your name and birth date are accurately recorded thereupon?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the document, the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the usher not -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um-hm, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether your name, your date of birth, are accurately reflected on this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just check whether the title of the case is correctly placed on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see that it is not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But let's -- we all understand that you do not have on your mind that there is a case of pseudonym versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a pseudonym sheet in the case Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm told in it's e-court now as 1D05302. So if we can pull it up and not broadcast the same, that could solve all of our issues, hopefully. But I think it will still have the wrong title, so we'll still need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are not going to change that, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be for the future to know what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There it goes. Now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I would ask for this document to be accepted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5302 receives number D830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I can now call up and again not broadcast 65 ter number 1D01703.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have a witness statement on the screen which is not being broadcast to the public. My first question to you: Do you recall giving this statement to the Defence team of General Mladic earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And whose signature is visible on this first page?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page of the document in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, whose signature is that we see on this page with the accompanying date in June of 2014?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature and the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to signing this written statement, did you have a chance to review the same in Serbian to verify that everything is correct in it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did and I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by everything as contained in your statement as being correctly recorded?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it's properly recorded and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to ask you today questions based on the same topics as covered in your statement, would your answers in substance be the same as recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be roughly the same. They wouldn't be different unless some elaboration were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now today, sir, you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth. Does that mean that the facts as contained in your statement are truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts are truthful and I made a solemn declaration to speak the truth before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the statement 1D01703 into evidence under seal. And mindful of Your Honour's instruction, I would leave the associated exhibits to be reviewed and for submissions to be made later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1703 receives number D831, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, given the protective measures I did not want to do a witness summary. I will just go straight to my remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: GRM130, first I'd like to look at paragraph 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is on page 2 of both languages and should not be broadcast. So if we could have page 2 of D831, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here in this paragraph you talk about how your barracks were blockaded by Croatian paramilitary forces. Can you please describe how you and other JNA members at the barracks felt during the blockade? What was the general mood and atmosphere as a result of the blockade?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I never expected that barracks could be under blockade, although there had been some hints that something was going on outside the barracks. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) Apart from that, you're invited to answer the question. The question was not whether you expected this to happen, what happened in your village, but how you felt; whereas your statement says that you were -- water-supply, food supply, and access to medical aid were cut off. So I think I would not feel very happy, rather miserable under those circumstances. And if that's what you felt then just say: "We felt miserable," instead of saying whether you expected it to happen or blockades. So could you please answer the question how did you feel under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was difficult to bear it in those circumstances. We had no power, no water, no supplies. We didn't have bread. We had very little food. It was very difficult to maintain the morale of our men because the nearest forces that were kindly disposed to us were about 50 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long did your barracks remain under the blockade from these Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We remained under blocked for exactly two months when fortunately a peaceful pullout was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could move to paragraph 8 of your statement, again not broadcasting the same. This is at page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so. Could you also tell us when this blockade took place, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991. Shall I give you the exact date? I know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Friday, 13 September, until 13 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 8 you talk about how your -- the barracks was attacked by the Croat National Guard many times, and though you had the ability to do it, no shell was ever fired at the neighbouring city. Can you please first tell us how many times and how you were attacked by the Croat National Guard?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those Croatian paramilitary forces that had just been formed attacked several times and created a number of incidents. However, there were three serious attacks on the barracks and a number of attacks at a separate building where we kept ammunition and explosives. Those attacks were the -- the first one was very fierce. The operation was called Deep and Peaceful Sleep. They were supposed to raid the barracks. We had with us some people who were working for the forces outside. They were supposed to create a commotion and chaos in order to make it so that the barracks would surrender. The surrounding forces were outnumbering us hugely and they moved in on the barracks from several directions. They started to infiltrate themselves through the shrubbery quietly. However, we used only infantry weapons and put up resistance. We did not use any large-calibre weapons, although we had them. And we had a lot of fire-power.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now can you explain to us what you mean when you say here that "no shell was ever fired at the city, even though the combat situation allowed for that"?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just after the blockade, we jointly took a decision - and everybody took part in that decision, from the youngest to the oldest and we made no -- we didn't look at rank - we decided that we would not leave the barracks and wait for a peaceful outcome. We decided not to create any incidents, not to fire shells at the city, because that would result in a huge conflict and nobody could know how that conflict would end. Under rules of engagement, we had the possibility of using large-calibre weapons, but we refrained ourselves. And I'm very proud of this because nobody was hurt except the attackers, and the property of the people who had been my fellow citizens until the day before was not damaged either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you quoted the witness as saying "not a single shell was fired at the city," but it's even more, even the surrounding. And if I understand the testimony of the witness well, that no shell at all was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's well understood. Now, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you just expand a little bit further on what you mean when you say "under the rules of engagement we had the possibility of using large-calibre weapons"?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our security was at risk, our safety was at risk. We did not leave the barracks and didn't intend to hurt anybody. Largely outnumbering forces were attacking us. In those circumstances, large-calibre weapons are normally used. And it's true that not a single shell was fired from the barracks in any direction. We didn't even throw a single grenade. We only used smaller-calibre infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to page 4 in both languages, again not broadcasting the same. And I'd like to look at paragraph number 13 with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, you talk about how the Muslim forces disrupted your supplies. Can you explain how they did that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mission of my unit was to secure that location, which you can see, point by important point. In 1992 there occurred some incidents on the ground between Muslim and Serb forces, and the Muslim forces - paramilitary forces - decided to block the supply of food and water at such points. This ceased very quickly and very fortunately we didn't need to use our arsenal to enable the resumption of supplies. This was arranged within a few days and we received food at its proper destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to paragraph 11, you state that your unit was tasked with separating the sides of the conflict. Can you explain how you did that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the Sava River, there occurred major incidents between Serb and Croat people. There were armed groups that created incidents between them, and we got the assignment to create a buffer zone between such forces. In the early days we were successful. We communicated more with the Serbian side because they were better disposed to us, and we didn't communicate with the Croat side until they began attacking us with artillery at first, followed by infantry attacks from Bosnia-Herzegovina territory. And that forced us at that moment to stay together with the Serb people who were there. I have to stress that in that period I had in my unit Muslim, Croat, Hungarian soldiers, people from Bunje [phoen], the Roma. And if you want to know the percentage, there were about 60 per cent Serbs. And for reasons that you well know, the others were less represented because their nations had appealed to them to withdraw from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask the witness to give a time-frame for paragraph 13 or paragraph 11. Could you give us a month and a year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After coming to Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 13th of November, we came to the said location and we were left in peace there for about a month or a month and a half before these incidents started. And the other location that is mentioned in the second place, all this was happening all the way until the VRS was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say 13th of November, you're referring to 13th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991 we arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then for about a month and a half we didn't have any incidents. And then the incidents began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand well that this was after Croatia had declared itself independent. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you're telling us about skirmishes, about conflicts. Were there attacks from Croatian territory or at least territory claimed by the newly established Croatian republic - and I'm not expressing myself on whether it was rightly done or not - to the territory which you considered to be BiH territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The attacks were launched from the territory of the Croatian state, from the other side of the Sava River. They began first with artillery and mortar attacks. And later, when infantry attacks were in full swing, they were also using multiple-rocket launchers, howitzers, and large-calibre weapons. I had the bad luck to have my defence showered twice in one day by a multiple-rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now move to page 6 and again not broadcast the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus there on paragraphs 23 through 24 of your statement. And here you talk of an attack on 26 June 1995 by Muslim forces from Srebrenica and Zepa upon Crna Rijeka and the VRS Main Staff. Can you please tell us first the tasking and strength or number of these forces from Zepa and Srebrenica that were involved in this attack?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true. On the 26th of June, along several axes from the so-called demilitarised zone, Muslim forces broke out and launched attacks. One was an attack at a village where they killed both the civilian population and the little number of fighting men who were there, and then they entered the sector of the Main Staff approaching at almost 300 metres. I didn't know exactly what forces were there, but it turned out later that there were 200 well-armed, well-trained soldiers sitting in ambush, and they were so brazen that they entered the Main Staff. At several other axes they cut off the roads Sokolac-Han Pijesak and Han Pijesak-Vlasenica in order to make it impossible for our supporting forces to come and assist us. We managed to push them back, and I can say now that it was only thanks to good luck and military ruse. On that occasion, I was very seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated that they came within 300 metres. Of what did they come within 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came 300 metres from the command of the Main Staff. They managed to get by our security and that's where they set up this ambush. They killed one soldier on that occasion and an officer was lightly wounded and he managed to alert the rest. I was with the Rapid Reaction Force when I went to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to another topic: General Mladic. How would you describe General Mladic as a commanding officer and as a person based upon your experiences?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met General Mladic personally, until then I had known of him, but I personally met him in 1993 as I was reassigned to serve on the Main Staff or, rather, one of these units. And several times I had an opportunity to communicate with him. We have rules of service in the army. The rules of service define what an officer should look like, how tidy an officer should be, how he should behave, and so on. If I were to assess General Mladic from that point of view, I would say that he was a true officer from the rules of service with all the required manners.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 6 in the English -- pardon me, page 7 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And look at paragraph number 27 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which, again, should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you state that every encounter with General Mladic was uncomfortable from the military point of view. Can you explain for us what you mean here?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that that's really the way it was, that encounters with General Mladic were uncomfortable but, on the other hand, a learning experience. It was uncomfortable because Mladic was very well versed in military affairs, the tactical use of units, the theory of warfare, the technical capacities of weapons, and he insisted that we commanders and komandirs should know this very well, too. In addition to that, he minded very much if soldiers were untidy. Also, he was very much against them leaving weapons aside and moving about without a weapon. He insisted that they should always have weapons. He would be upset if they did not have their combat kits on them. Also the discomfort was as follows: When soldiers returned from their assignments, then they would relax in base a bit. However, he insisted on work and order. He also insisted that we should know each and every soldier personally and that we should know what his abilities were, also whether he was married, what kind of family he had, and he would check that very quickly with a few questions. And he would look at the officer concerned and if the officer exhibited any discomfort, that meant that he did not feel certain and sure of himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 6 in the English, page 5 in the Serbian, and focus on paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here, sir, you describe how General Mladic managed to recover the combat morale of troops in a particular location. What did he do to recover the combat morale of those troops and permit them to take over that particular location listed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it is sufficient for the superior officer to show up as a person who has authority, and that is sufficient motivation for carrying out a mission. In that period of time, General Mladic had a huge reputation in the Serb army. As soon as he appeared and talked to soldiers, it was like infusion for a sick person, and this immediately boosted the morale of the soldiers. The soldiers were ready for combat. He saw that there was decisiveness among the commanders. Because, you know, it is not easy to motivate people to move and face the possibility of being hit by a bullet. A person has to be well-prepared for that, the morale has to be high in order to set out on such a mission, and a person should know why he is doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, as a career military officer yourself, what other sorts of things can a commander do to ensure that the morale of soldiers is at an appropriate level?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, one has to give one's own example at a high level. There should be honour and honesty at a high level so that people would be willing to follow such an officer. Also, such an officer has to be familiar with the rules and regulations. However, the rules and regulations amount to nothing if one doesn't have leadership qualities. As far as commanders were concerned, it was important to know how to wage war, how to conduct one's self in difficult situations. We all had to improvise. The soldiers appreciated us to the degree to which we were capable of responding to a newly created situation that was usually complicated. We needed to make rational moves and to accomplish the mission involved with the least number of casualties. Also, how to resort to ruse in warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you finished your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of my team, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we have a look at Exhibit P02120.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what you will see come up here is a 13 July 1995 order from General Mladic. You can see that in full on the B/C/S. And it's addressed to the Drina Corps, the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, amongst others. Now it's -- we see from the heading of this order that it deals with the prevention and leakage of military secrets in the area of combat operations. And I'll just highlight a few of those. Under item 1 in the order, the order is to prevent the entry of all uninvited individuals to the general sector of Srebrenica and Zepa. If you follow me down to item 4, it talks about preventing the entry of local and foreign journalists, except those authorised by the Main Staff, to the wider areas of Srebrenica and Zepa. And then if we follow through to item 5, what you see at the bottom there talks about banning and preventing the giving of information in relation to combat operation as well as to the overall activities involving prisoners of war and others. Have you seen this order from General Mladic before?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had the opportunity. Those who are familiar with the hierarchy that existed in all armies of the world would know that such orders could not reach me, except for an order that pertains exactly to my unit -- rather, the unit that I command. I get excerpts from an order if something pertains to me. I had the role of reserve for the Main Staff and I did not have such tasks. This was usually something that units that covered a broader area had. You can see all the places referred to here. I never had such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 26041.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we look at that, were you aware of the order of that -- that this was ordered, apart from whether you have seen it? Because that was the simple question: Did you see it? Apparently you did not. Were you aware of in any way of the content of what was ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of the content at all. From a professional point of view, tasks are given only to those who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you have answered the question. You were not aware of the content of the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at this document. It's another order. It's dated the 15th of July. And it's from Milomir Savcic and signed for him by Jovo Jazic. And Jovo Jazic, he was Colonel Savcic's deputy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was deputy commander and chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness, was there anything you would like to bring to my attention? I saw you raising your hand. And if so, could you tell us whether we could hear it in open session or whether you would like to go in private session for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be heard in open session. I just want a clarification. Considering that I felt a certain mistrust in what I'm saying, I can provide a document, which I believe I have in my hotel room, as proof to remove any shade of doubt. And I'm sorry this happened. I was talking about the month of June. I didn't realise you were talking about July. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether I fully understand it. The main issue was that we would like to have specific data, that is, not approximately this or I went there, but to say when did you go anywhere, what happened, et cetera, and we were mainly interested in chronology rather than in the content of medical treatment. That's one. Second, when you say you were talking about the month of June, we understood that something happened in June which kept you out of business for, as you said, three months of which we now received further details about your whereabouts during those three months. And there is -- unless the parties would have any need to further explore the matter, then we do not need any further documentation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 26041 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26041 receives number P6957, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Ivetic, do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. And if we can go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness GRM130, we have concluded hearing your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, and I wish you a safe return home again. If you could please wait for a second and not yet leave the courtroom because we have to turn into closed session for that again, because I would already announce that we'll adjourn at this very point in time because there is no -- the next witness is not available -- or is the next witness available?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The next witness is in the waiting room, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's the case, then we turn into closed session and we'll -- and the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bilbija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, we have only ten minutes left today, so it will be only after the weekend that we'll hear most of your evidence but we nevertheless thought it good to start already. You'll first be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: Simo Bilbija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would ask that 65 ter number 1D1757 be shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have a witness statement on the screen. The first question I have for you, Doctor: Do you remember giving such a statement to General Mladic's Defence team earlier this year?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the record, can you confirm for us whose signature is visible on this page?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, could you tell us whose signature is on this page of the document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: Again, this is my signature, the 28th of July, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to turn to page 5 in both versions, and I would like to look at paragraph number 20 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would like to ask you do you have any corrections to be made to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: I think that for the sake of the truth it would be of interest to correct a sentence. The one in the third line: His character of an honourable, righteous, and brave soldier, he would prove it every day. That could mean that we saw each other every day. Maybe it would be better to say "every time when we were together" and so on, rather than "every day."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Apart from this one clarification, do you stand by everything else that is contained in the written statement as written as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I stand by everything that is written here. I fully stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, if I were to ask you questions today arising out of the same facts and topics as in your written statement, would your answers today be in substance the same as recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: My answers would be the same in terms of the essence and in terms of the details involved as contained in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Doctor, insofar as you have taken a solemn declaration today, this afternoon, would those answers as contained in your statement be truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: Of course they would be truthful. That's what we've said, the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the statement 1D1757 as the next public exhibit. There are no associated exhibits to this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1757 receives number D832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Any further questions or do you first want to read the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should read the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simo Bilbija transferred from Croatia to the Sokolac military hospital at the end of May 1992. He remained there until September of 1993 when he transferred to the Banja Luka military medical centre. At Sokolac military hospital, the staff was ethnically mixed. There were also soldiers and civilians at the hospital of Muslim and Croat ethnicity. General Mladic insisted wounded enemy soldiers should be provided medical assistance without any discrimination. General Mladic also ordered Dr. Bilbija to fly to Srebrenica to provide medical assistance to a Canadian soldier. In April 1993, the witness participated in a medivac evacuation of people from Srebrenica. General Mladic ordered him to execute this task in a fair manner and in accord with medical ethics. In relation to General Mladic, Dr. Bilbija says the General, on every occasion they met, proved his character as an honourable, righteous, and brave soldier. That completes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any further questions, we could start. But we have only three or four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Sokolac hospital, to what organisation was that hospital directly subordinated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'm looking at the text of your summary and it seems to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that there is an error that managed to slip in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the summary is not evidence. So if there are any mistakes, of course we try to avoid them, but the evidence is what is found in your statement. So don't bother about the summary. We will rely on your statement, not on that summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, Doctor, if I could ask you the -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: The hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. To what organisation was the Sokolac hospital directly subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: The hospital in Sokolac where I worked was called the hospital of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, so it was directly subordinated to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The medical staff in this hospital mostly hailed from Sarajevo, from the military hospital of Sarajevo and other hospitals, other civilian hospitals in Sarajevo. I myself hailed from the military hospital in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can briefly turn to paragraph 8, found on page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph you state that the staff at Sokolac hospital was of mixed ethnicity. Was that true for the duration of your time spent there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA
utterances.text: As I have mentioned, the staff at the hospital came from the military hospital in Sarajevo. Most of them. And the rest were doctors and other medical staff from different hospitals in Sarajevo. Their ethnic background was mixed. What is characteristic of this hospital is that all the medical staff who wished to co-operate were gladly taken in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they wanted to leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. Could you please focus on the question, whether the composition remained mixed during all the time you were working there, because that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, mixed throughout this period. In the beginning of the war, there were several members of the medical staff that came and left the hospital but some stayed on. Dr. Ljubo Berberian, I can mention him, he is a neurosurgeon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it looks as if you have received an answer to your question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless you would like to know exactly who was there which would --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we could just have the completion of Dr. Berberian, what his ethnicity was, and then we can pause for the day since we are at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So finish your answer, although it wasn't asked to deal with specific persons, tell us about Dr. Berberian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Berberian originally came from an Armenian family in Sarajevo. His mother was Turkish. At the time when we worked in that hospital, his mother and his brother were still in Sarajevo. And this doctor stayed at the Sokolac hospital throughout the war, the hospital of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day. Witness, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is the testimony already given today, that also includes of course your statement, or whether that's testimony still to be given on Monday, because we resume on Monday at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom. Therefore, we would like to see you back on Monday morning and you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume Monday, the 1st of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
